about: The featured moments of "the world at a moment", and what this project can say about each region at each of them. An entry either POINTS AT one of the map’s own dated anchors, or is a sourced entry from the pass of 2026-11-27, or states that nobody has looked, or states a finding about the record itself.
rules: Part B rules: real sources, a tier on every claim, nothing typed without a source. A sourced entry here is NOT added to the map’s 565 anchors: that is an approved set and growing it is its own ruling.
regions: North Africa and the Near East

moments.title: The crucifixion
moments.why: An execution almost every scholar accepts happened, on a year nobody can fix: 30 and 33 CE both fit Pilate’s prefecture and the gospels’ own calendar notes. THE TIER IS ABOUT THE DATE, NOT THE EVENT.

Oceania.finding: The settled record pauses here, and that is a measured result rather than a gap in our reading.
Oceania.detail: West Polynesia is settled by c. 800 BCE and then nothing moves east for about eighteen hundred years. At this moment the Pacific frontier is where it was eight centuries ago.
Oceania.source: Wilmshurst, J.M., Hunt, T.L., Lipo, C.P. & Anderson, A.J., “High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia”, PNAS 108, 2011, 1815–1820 — 1,434 dates from at least 45 islands. Migration into East Polynesia begins only after a 1,800-year PAUSE following the settlement of Samoa c. 800 BC, in two phases: the Society Islands c. 1025–1120 CE, the rest c. 1190–1290 CE. Mulrooney et al., PNAS 108, 2011, E192, dispute the statistics while accepting the late chronology.

the Americas.label: Cahuachi, the Nasca ceremonial centre
the Americas.source: Cahuachi, the Nasca ceremonial centre: Silverman, H., Cahuachi in the Ancient Nasca World, covering c. 200 BC – AD 600, with Orefici’s excavations showing it was not a permanent domestic settlement. Conlee, C. et al. compile 770 radiocarbon dates from more than 60 south-coast sites against the ceramic phase chronology.
the Americas.note: In use through this century; a ceremonial centre rather than a city, which is itself the finding.

Europe.label: Rome under Tiberius
Europe.source: Tiberius, Roman emperor 14–37 CE (Encyclopædia Britannica). The reign is among the best-attested facts of the period and the panel treats it as such.
Europe.note: The prefect who tried the case answers to this emperor, which is the only reason the year can be argued at all.

North Africa and the Near East.label: Kush and Rome, after the treaty of Samos
North Africa and the Near East.source: The treaty between Kush and Rome agreed on Samos in 21/20 BCE (22 BC in some accounts), after Amanirenas’ war with Petronius; Augustus withdrew the frontier to Hiere Sycaminos and Kush paid no tribute. The bronze head of Augustus found buried beneath a temple step at Meroë (Garstang, 1910) is the physical end of that episode.
North Africa and the Near East.note: Meroë is a generation past its war with Rome and paying no tribute. The buried head of Augustus is the object that dates it.

North Africa and the Near East.label: Parthia under Artabanus II
North Africa and the Near East.source: Artabanus II of Parthia, r. c. 12–38/40 CE. The regnal dates are reconstructed from coins and from Tacitus and Josephus, and scholars differ by several years at both ends, so the tier is contested.
North Africa and the Near East.note: The empire between Rome and India, and the regnal dates are reconstructed rather than recorded.

Southeast Asia.label: Cổ Loa, the rampart ditch in use
Southeast Asia.source: Kim, N.C., Lai Van Toi & Trinh Hoang Hiep, “Co Loa: an investigation of Vietnam’s ancient capital”, Antiquity 84 (326), 2010, 1011–1027. Rampart Phase 3 layers 396–170 cal BC; charcoal from the ditch 103 BC – cal AD 67.
Southeast Asia.note: Charcoal from the ditch calibrates to 103 BC – cal AD 67, which brackets this moment. The dates bound ACTIVITY and not the first digging, which the excavators say in those words.

Southeast Asia.label: Lai Nghi, a Sa Huỳnh jar-burial cemetery
Southeast Asia.source: Reinecke, A. & Lâm Thị Mỹ Dung on the Lai Nghi cemetery (Quảng Nam): IPPA Bulletin 29, 2009, 68–75, and Lâm Thị Mỹ Dung, “The Sa Huynh Culture in Ancient Regional Trade Networks”, Terra Australis 45, 2017. One jar 2086±50 BP (Erl-5995); the cemetery calibrates to the 3rd century BC – 1st century AD.
Southeast Asia.note: Iron, glass and carnelian from a coastal trade network, in use across this moment.

Southeast Asia.label: Óc Eo begins
Southeast Asia.source: Wang, W. et al., “Earliest curry in Southeast Asia and the global spice trade 2000 years ago”, Science Advances 9, 2023, eadh5517. The radiocarbon dates place the major occupation of Óc Eo between the 1st and 8th centuries CE; one sample calibrates to 207–326 cal CE.
Southeast Asia.note: The port the Chinese sources call Funan. The occupation runs from the 1st to the 8th century CE; WHERE INSIDE THE 1ST CENTURY IT STARTS IS NOT FIXED, and the earliest dated sample is later.

South Asia.label: Kujula Kadphises founds the Kushan empire
South Asia.source: Kujula Kadphises, founder of the Kushan empire, reign estimated c. 25–85 CE. THE CHRONOLOGY IS UNSETTLED: the Rabatak inscription fixes the dynasty’s genealogy but not its absolute dates, and the start of the Kanishka era is placed at 127 CE on Harry Falk’s work or at 78 CE on the older view, which is still argued (Sino-Platonic Papers 227, 2012).
South Asia.note: Begram and the Kabul valley. The dynasty is certain and its absolute chronology is argued over a fifty-year range.

East Asia.label: The Han restored, the capital at Luoyang
East Asia.source: Guangwu, who restored the Han in 25 CE and moved the capital to Luoyang, r. 25–57 CE (Encyclopædia Britannica).
East Asia.note: Guangwu takes the throne in 25 CE and moves the capital east. The empire at the other end of Eurasia from Tiberius.

moments.title: The Younger Dryas begins
moments.why: An abrupt return to near-glacial cold, dated in the Greenland ice cores. Göbekli Tepe’s world is on the far side of it.

moments.title: The Great Pyramid
moments.why: The one date in this list most readers already own.

East Asia.label: Longshan, the late phase
East Asia.source: The Longshan sequence of the middle and lower Yellow River, c. 3000–1900 BC, late phase c. 2600–2000 BC, on the Bayesian review of Chinese Neolithic radiocarbon dates held at the University of Oxford (ora.ox.ac.uk). The review states its own caveat: the dated samples do not necessarily catch the earliest and latest phases, so the boundaries are approximations.
East Asia.note: Walled towns of rammed earth across the Yellow River plain, at the type site of Chengziya. The phase boundaries are approximations and the review that gives them says so.

East Asia.label: Shijiahe, on the middle Yangtze
East Asia.source: Shijiahe on the middle Yangtze, c. 2500–2000 BC, with Qujialing before it at c. 3400–2500 BC, from the same Oxford Bayesian review. Contemporary with Liangzhu and culturally distinct from it.
East Asia.note: A walled centre contemporary with Liangzhu and culturally distinct from it.

Oceania.detail: Lapita has not left the Bismarck Archipelago yet; the open Pacific is a thousand years away and East Polynesia three thousand five hundred.
Oceania.source: Wilmshurst, J.M., Hunt, T.L., Lipo, C.P. & Anderson, A.J., “High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia”, PNAS 108, 2011, 1815–1820 — 1,434 dates from at least 45 islands. Migration into East Polynesia begins only after a 1,800-year PAUSE following the settlement of Samoa c. 800 BC, in two phases: the Society Islands c. 1025–1120 CE, the rest c. 1190–1290 CE. Mulrooney et al., PNAS 108, 2011, E192, dispute the statistics while accepting the late chronology.
